nodes.title: Security fundamentals: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Security is about layering defenses so no single failure compromises a system. Most exams test the same core ideas: least privilege, defense in depth, the CIA triad, and the shared-responsibility line between you and your cloud provider.

flashcards.front: What is the CIA triad?
flashcards.back: Confidentiality (only the right people see the data), Integrity (data isn't tampered with), Availability (the system is reachable when needed). Every security control maps to at least one of these three pillars.

flashcards.front: What does 'least privilege' mean?
flashcards.back: Grant each identity (user, role, service account) the minimum permissions needed to do its job — no more. The opposite is wildcard access, which makes a single credential leak catastrophic.

flashcards.front: What is defense in depth?
flashcards.back: Stack multiple, independent controls so an attacker has to defeat all of them. Example: WAF in front of an app, network ACL on the subnet, IAM on the workload, encryption at rest in the database.

flashcards.front: Shared responsibility model — who does what?
flashcards.back: The cloud provider secures the cloud (physical hardware, hypervisor, region facilities). You secure what's IN the cloud (your data, IAM config, OS patching on EC2, application code). The exact line shifts by service: serverless is more on the provider, IaaS is more on you.

questions.q: An EC2 instance must be granted read-only permission to a specific S3 bucket. Best practice in AWS is to attach a ROLE with the minimum permissions to the instance, not store an access key on disk. Which AWS service models who/what can do what on AWS resources via users, groups, roles, and policies?
choices: AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) — users, groups, roles, and policies that authorise actions on AWS resources, including instance-attached roles for EC2
AWS Internet Access Management — not a real AWS service name; no IAM-like role-attachment mechanism exists under this fabricated label
AWS Infrastructure and Application Management — not a real AWS service name; identity, permissions, and EC2-role attachment live in IAM
AWS Image and AMI Management — not a real AWS service name; AMIs themselves are templates and do not provide identity or access management
questions.explanation: IAM (Identity and Access Management) controls authentication (who you are) and authorization (what you can do) in AWS through users, groups, roles, and policies.

questions.q: A security audit asks: who made an `iam:DeleteUser` call against the production account at 14:47 UTC yesterday, from which IP, with which user-agent, and what parameters were used? The answer must come from the tenant-wide management-plane log. Which AWS service?
choices: Amazon CloudWatch — aggregates metrics and application logs; not the canonical tenant-wide control-plane audit trail of every AWS API call against the account
AWS CloudFormation — declarative IaC engine that provisions stacks from templates; not the tenant-wide audit log of every AWS API call against the account
AWS Transit Gateway — central networking hub for VPC and on-prem connectivity; not the tenant-wide audit log of every AWS API call against the account
AWS CloudTrail — tenant-wide control-plane audit log: who called the API, when, from which IP, with which user-agent, and with what request parameters
questions.explanation: CloudTrail records all API calls made to AWS services, providing an audit log of who did what, when, and from where. Essential for compliance and security investigations.

questions.q: A security investigator needs a per-API-call record: WHO (IAM principal), WHEN (timestamp), FROM WHERE (source IP / user-agent), WHAT (API name), WITH WHAT (request parameters). This is the AWS API auditing surface — distinct from metrics/logs aggregated by CloudWatch. Which AWS service provides exactly this audit trail?
choices: AWS CloudTrail — records every API call across the account with caller identity, timestamp, source IP, user-agent, and request parameters captured in JSON events
AWS Inspector — automated vulnerability assessment of EC2, Lambda, and ECR workloads; not the per-API-call audit log of who called what, when, from where
AWS Config — resource-configuration history and rule evaluation over time; not the per-API-call audit log of who called what, when, from where, with parameters
Amazon CloudWatch — metrics and application log aggregation surface; useful for observability but not the per-API-call audit log of who called what, when
questions.explanation: CloudTrail is the AWS API-call audit log: every `Action` against any service is recorded with caller identity, time, source IP, user-agent, and parameters. CloudWatch is metrics + log aggregation — not the per-API audit trail. PRIOR VERSION HAD WRONG CORRECT-ANSWER INDEX (marked CloudWatch) — fixed 2026-05-13.

questions.q: A security team wants to grant the IAM principal `arn:aws:iam::111:role/web` access to a specific S3 bucket and deny everyone else. The control is written as a JSON document attached to the bucket itself (not to any IAM identity). Which control type is this?
choices: An S3 bucket policy — a JSON resource policy attached to the bucket; the canonical mechanism for bucket-level allow/deny grants against IAM principals
An EC2 instance profile — attaches an IAM role to an EC2 instance; not a bucket-side allow/deny control attached to the S3 bucket as a resource
An S3 lifecycle policy — transitions or expires objects between storage classes; not an access-control mechanism that allows or denies principals
Default bucket encryption — encrypts new objects at rest with the configured key; not an access-control mechanism that allows or denies principals
questions.explanation: S3 bucket policies are JSON-based resource policies that control who can access a bucket and what actions they can perform. They can grant access to other AWS accounts.

questions.q: A security architect drafts IAM policy for a new EC2 role. The role's job is to read ONE specific S3 bucket. Best practice says grant nothing beyond that exact need — not full S3, not even read on all buckets. Which IAM principle is this?
choices: Least privilege — grant the MINIMUM permissions needed for the task
Broad admin access — explicitly the opposite of best practice
Shared IAM user across the team — anti-pattern; no audit per person
Long-lived access keys on users — anti-pattern; prefer assumable roles
questions.explanation: The principle of least privilege means granting only the permissions necessary to perform a task — nothing more. This minimizes the blast radius of compromised credentials.

questions.q: A Lambda function must read from DynamoDB and write to S3. The team wants AWS BEST PRACTICE for credentials: NO long-lived access keys baked into the function code or env vars; AWS auto-injects temporary credentials when the function runs. Which IAM construct does this?
choices: IAM User with access keys — long-lived, anti-pattern for compute identity
IAM Role assumed via STS — short-lived temporary credentials auto-vended to the Lambda execution environment
IAM Group — a collection of users, cannot itself execute code or assume permissions
IAM Policy document — describes permissions, but is attached to a principal (user/role/group), not used directly
questions.explanation: IAM Roles are assumable identities with permissions. EC2 instances, Lambda functions, and cross-account users assume roles. No static credentials — uses temporary security tokens via STS.

questions.q: All web traffic must be encrypted in transit. The certificate that proves the server's identity and enables TLS handshakes must be (a) trusted by every modern browser, (b) issued / renewed automatically by AWS at no cost, (c) usable on ALB + CloudFront + API GW. Which AWS service issues these public TLS certs?
choices: AWS Trusted Advisor — provides best-practice checks and cost recommendations; it does NOT issue public TLS certificates for ALB, CloudFront, or API Gateway
AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) — issues and auto-renews free public TLS certificates for use on ALB, CloudFront, API Gateway, and other integrated services
AWS Secrets Manager — stores and rotates secrets such as DB passwords; it does NOT issue public TLS certificates for ALB, CloudFront, or API Gateway
AWS KMS — manages encryption keys for data at rest across AWS services; it does NOT issue public TLS certificates for ALB, CloudFront, or API Gateway
questions.explanation: HTTPS uses TLS/SSL for encryption. AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) provisions and manages free public SSL/TLS certificates for use with ELB, CloudFront, and API Gateway.

questions.q: A public-facing web tier is hit with a sustained Layer-3/4 volumetric DDoS (SYN floods, UDP reflection). The customer wants automatic, no-config-required L3/L4 DDoS protection AT NO ADDITIONAL CHARGE; for the higher tier (cost-protection guarantees, DDoS Response Team access) they're willing to pay extra. Which service provides this?
choices: AWS Shield (Standard = free, Advanced = paid) — L3/L4 DDoS protection at the AWS edge, automatic for all customers with no configuration required
AWS WAF — Layer-7 HTTP rules engine on top of ALB / API Gateway / CloudFront; not a Layer-3/4 volumetric DDoS protection service
AWS KMS — managed encryption-key service used for encrypt/decrypt operations on customer data; unrelated to L3/L4 DDoS protection
AWS Certificate Manager — issues and renews TLS certificates for AWS-integrated endpoints; unrelated to L3/L4 DDoS protection
questions.explanation: AWS Shield Standard: free, automatic DDoS protection for all AWS customers. Shield Advanced: paid, enhanced protection for EC2, ELB, CloudFront, Route 53 with the DDoS Response Team (DRT) and financial protection.

nodes.title: Networking fundamentals: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Networking moves packets between machines using layered protocols (the OSI / TCP-IP stack). Most exam questions test routing decisions, subnetting math, the difference between L2 and L3, and how DNS / DHCP make the whole thing usable for humans.

flashcards.front: What's the difference between Layer 2 and Layer 3?
flashcards.back: L2 (data link) uses MAC addresses to deliver frames inside a single broadcast domain (a switch). L3 (network) uses IP addresses to route packets between networks (a router). Switches do L2; routers do L3.

flashcards.front: How does a subnet mask work?
flashcards.back: The mask splits an IP into a network portion (the high bits, set to 1) and a host portion (the low bits, set to 0). `/24` means the first 24 bits are network = up to 256 hosts (254 usable). `/30` is 4 IPs = 2 hosts — typical for a point-to-point link.

flashcards.front: What does DNS do?
flashcards.back: Domain Name System translates human-readable names (`example.com`) into IP addresses. A recursive resolver asks the root, the TLD server (`.com`), and finally the authoritative server for the domain. TTL controls how long answers are cached.

flashcards.front: TCP vs UDP — when do you pick each?
flashcards.back: TCP is reliable, ordered, congestion-controlled — use it when every byte matters (HTTP, SSH, SMTP). UDP is lightweight, no handshake, no retransmit — use it for streaming, gaming, DNS queries, anywhere latency beats reliability.

questions.q: A streaming site serves 90% static assets (videos, images) and is hit by viral traffic spikes from specific countries. Latency to those geographies dominates user-perceived performance. Which AWS service caches the assets at edge locations close to viewers and absorbs the spike load before it reaches the origin?
choices: Amazon Route 53 — DNS routing service; resolves names to endpoints but does not cache asset bytes at hundreds of edge POPs near viewers around the world
AWS Site-to-Site VPN — encrypted tunnel between on-prem and AWS for corporate traffic; not a global CDN that caches static asset bytes near viewers
Application Load Balancer — regional Layer-7 load balancer at the origin Region; does not cache static asset bytes at hundreds of edge POPs near viewers
Amazon CloudFront — global CDN with 600+ edge POPs caching static asset bytes near viewers, with regional origin shielding and TLS termination at the edge
questions.explanation: Amazon CloudFront is a CDN that distributes content from edge locations worldwide, reducing latency for end users by serving cached content from the nearest edge location.

questions.q: An architect designs a NETWORK construct inside an AWS account that has customer-defined private IP ranges (CIDR), customer-defined subnets per AZ, route tables, NACLs, and security groups. The construct is LOGICALLY ISOLATED from other accounts. Which AWS resource is this?
choices: An EC2 instance — a single virtual machine that runs inside a network; not the customer-defined CIDR/subnet/route-table network construct described in the question
The AWS global backbone — AWS's private inter-Region network plumbing; customers cannot define CIDR ranges, subnets, route tables, NACLs, or security groups on it
A Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) — customer-defined logically isolated virtual network with CIDR, subnets per AZ, route tables, NACLs, and security groups
Amazon EKS — managed Kubernetes control plane that runs inside a VPC; the VPC is the network construct, not EKS itself
questions.explanation: A VPC is the canonical AWS virtual network primitive: customer-defined IP ranges, subnets per AZ, route tables, NACLs, SGs, gateways. PRIOR VERSION HAD A MISMATCH between the stem (about steady-state pricing) and the marked-correct answer (about VPC). Rewritten for consistency 2026-05-13.

questions.q: A workload's web tier in a public subnet needs bidirectional internet connectivity. The route table for that subnet must have a default route pointing at a VPC-level component. Which component fits this role?
choices: Internet Gateway — VPC-level horizontally scaled component that allows bidirectional internet ingress and egress for resources in a public subnet with a default route
VPC Peering — links two VPCs privately over the AWS backbone with no internet path; does not provide bidirectional internet connectivity for public-subnet resources
Network ACL — stateless subnet-level firewall that filters packets at subnet boundaries; not the VPC-level gateway component used for bidirectional internet routing
NAT Gateway — egress-only NAT for resources in private subnets to reach the internet; not bidirectional internet connectivity for resources in a public subnet
questions.explanation: An Internet Gateway (IGW) is a horizontally-scaled, redundant VPC component that enables communication between VPC instances and the internet.

questions.q: A team needs to (a) register a `.com` domain, (b) host an authoritative DNS zone, (c) route users by geolocation/latency/weighted policies, (d) integrate health checks for failover. Which AWS service?
choices: Amazon S3 + CloudFront — object storage and CDN; useful for static content but neither registers domains nor serves authoritative DNS records
Amazon Route 53 — registers `.com` domains AND hosts authoritative DNS with routing policies (weighted, geolocation, failover, latency) and health checks
AWS Direct Connect + VPC peering — private network connectivity primitives; do not register domains or host authoritative DNS records
AWS Global Accelerator — anycast IP traffic acceleration; routes existing traffic but neither registers domains nor hosts DNS zone records
questions.explanation: Route 53 is AWS's scalable DNS service. It routes users to applications, supports health checks, and offers routing policies like latency, geolocation, and failover.

questions.q: A web-server EC2 instance must accept HTTPS (TCP 443) from anywhere and SSH (TCP 22) only from the office IP. The control is a STATEFUL allow-only firewall attached to the instance's ENI, where outbound replies are auto-permitted by state. Which AWS control is this?
choices: Network ACL — stateless, subnet-level, supports both allow and deny rules evaluated by rule number; not the stateful instance-attached allow-only control
EC2 Security Group — stateful, instance-level (per-ENI), allow-only rules with no explicit deny; the canonical stateful instance-attached firewall control
IAM group — controls IAM administrator actions and policy attachment; not a firewall that filters HTTPS or SSH packets reaching an EC2 instance
VPC route table entry — controls how packets are routed between subnets and gateways; not a firewall that filters HTTPS or SSH packets per instance
questions.explanation: Security Groups are stateful (return traffic automatically allowed) instance-level firewalls. You define allow rules only — there are no deny rules. Compare with Network ACLs which are stateless and subnet-level.

questions.q: An architect compares two VPC firewall constructs: (A) stateful, attached to ENIs, ALLOW-only, evaluates rules together; (B) stateless, attached to subnets, can ALLOW or DENY, evaluates rules in numbered order. Which mapping is correct?
choices: Security Groups and NACLs are identical and only the console UI differs between them — false; they have different statefulness, attachment, and rule semantics
Security Group = stateful, instance-level, allow-only with implicit deny; NACL = stateless, subnet-level, allow + deny rules evaluated in numbered order
NACLs are instance-level and Security Groups are subnet-level — reversed; SGs are instance-level (per-ENI) and NACLs are subnet-level associations
SGs evaluate outbound only and NACLs evaluate inbound only — false; both Security Groups and NACLs apply to inbound and outbound directions
questions.explanation: SG: stateful (return traffic auto-allowed), instance level, allow rules only, evaluated as a whole. NACL: stateless (return traffic needs explicit rule), subnet level, ordered allow/deny rules. instance-level, allow-only rules. Network ACLs: stateless, subnet-level, allow AND deny rules

questions.q: EC2 instances in a PRIVATE subnet need OUTBOUND internet access (e.g., to call SaaS APIs and pull OS updates) WITHOUT being directly reachable from the internet inbound. Which VPC component provides outbound-only NAT for private subnets?
choices: VPC Peering — links two VPCs privately; no internet path
NAT Gateway — managed NAT service: private-subnet outbound to internet via Elastic IP, NO inbound
Internet Gateway — bidirectional ingress/egress, NOT outbound-only
Virtual Private Gateway (VGW) — terminates IPsec VPN tunnels from on-prem; this is a different service from NAT GW
questions.explanation: NAT Gateway = managed outbound-only NAT for private subnets, billed per hour + per GB. Internet Gateway = bidirectional. Virtual Private Gateway = IPsec VPN termination (a completely different service). PRIOR VERSION HAD WRONG CORRECT-ANSWER INDEX (marked VPN termination as the NAT GW definition) — fixed 2026-05-13.

questions.q: A multi-region application wants ANYCAST IP entry points: users globally connect to a single static IP that the AWS network routes over its backbone to the closest healthy regional endpoint, with sub-second failover on regional health degradation. Which service?
choices: Amazon CloudFront — content-delivery network that caches HTTP responses at edge POPs; not a static-anycast-IP backbone-routing front door
Amazon Route 53 — DNS service with routing policies; relies on resolver caching, not anycast IPs that route over the AWS backbone
AWS Global Accelerator — two static anycast IPs that route over the AWS backbone to the closest healthy regional endpoint of the application
Application Load Balancer — regional Layer-7 load balancer scoped to one Region; not a global anycast entry point routing across multiple Regions
questions.explanation: Global Accelerator uses AWS's private global network (not the internet) to route traffic to the optimal regional endpoint, reducing latency and improving failover for global applications.

nodes.title: Cloud fundamentals (CLF-C02 / AZ-900 / CCNA): Key Ideas
nodes.content: Cloud fundamentals questions appear on almost every entry-level certification. They test your ability to map a business requirement to the correct service model (IaaS/PaaS/SaaS), understand the provider vs customer responsibility split, and compare on-premises capex to cloud opex — all before any technical deep-dive.

flashcards.front: IaaS vs PaaS vs SaaS — who manages what in each model?
flashcards.back: IaaS (EC2, Azure VM, Compute Engine): provider manages hardware + hypervisor; you manage OS, runtime, app, data. PaaS (App Service, Elastic Beanstalk, App Engine): provider adds OS + runtime; you manage app + data. SaaS (Office 365, Salesforce): provider manages everything; you manage user config and data. As you move up the stack you trade control for speed.

flashcards.front: Shared responsibility model — where is the exact dividing line?
flashcards.back: The provider is always responsible for security OF the cloud (physical data centers, networking fabric, hypervisor, managed service software). The customer is always responsible for security IN the cloud (data classification, IAM configuration, OS patching on IaaS VMs, application code). The dividing line shifts up the stack for PaaS and SaaS — the more managed the service, the more the provider owns.

flashcards.front: Regions vs Availability Zones — what is each?
flashcards.back: A region is a geographic cluster of data centers (e.g., us-east-1, West Europe). An AZ is one or more discrete data centers within a region with independent power, cooling, and networking. AZs in a region are close enough for low-latency synchronous replication but far enough apart that a fire/flood in one doesn't hit another. Spread workloads across at least 2 AZs for high availability.

flashcards.front: Capex vs opex — why does cloud shift the spending model?
flashcards.back: Capex (capital expenditure): large upfront purchase of hardware that you then depreciate over years; on-premises servers. Opex (operating expenditure): ongoing pay-as-you-go cost; cloud compute bills. Cloud converts infra from capex to opex — no hardware procurement lead times, costs scale with actual usage, easier to budget for a startup or to kill a failed project without a sunk-cost legacy.

questions.q: An auditor asks who is responsible for hypervisor patching, physical-data-centre security, customer's EC2 guest OS hardening, and customer's IAM-policy design. The customer answers with one model published by AWS. Which is the correct division?
choices: AWS manages every layer of the stack — hardware, hypervisor, network, guest OS, customer applications, IAM, and data — leaving customers no operational duties
Customers run physical datacentre security and operate the AWS global backbone network, while AWS only provisions virtual machines from the customer-built fleet
AWS secures the cloud (hardware, hypervisor, facilities, global network); customers secure what they put IN the cloud (data, IAM, guest OS, application config)
AWS handles every compliance and regulatory requirement transparently for the customer, with no shared duties on data, identity, or operating-system configuration
questions.explanation: AWS is responsible for security OF the cloud (hardware, facilities, global infrastructure). Customers are responsible for security IN the cloud (data, IAM, OS patching on EC2, etc.).

questions.q: A startup wants the LOWEST latency for users in Tokyo, São Paulo, and Frankfurt. The architect proposes deploying the same application stack in AWS Regions geographically close to each user population (e.g., ap-northeast-1, sa-east-1, eu-central-1). What is the PRIMARY benefit of using these distinct Regions?
choices: Lower latency to nearby users PLUS regional data-residency for local regulations — the genuine benefit of multi-Region geographic deployment
Automatic synchronous replication of all services across every Region by default — FALSE; cross-Region replication is opt-in per service and is NEVER 'default'
Identical published prices across every Region — FALSE; per-Region pricing varies
Free inter-Region data transfer for active-active workloads — FALSE; inter-Region transfer is billable
questions.explanation: Deploying into geographically closer Regions reduces latency for nearby users and supports data-residency requirements. AWS does NOT automatically replicate services across Regions; each service requires explicit configuration (S3 CRR, DynamoDB Global Tables, etc.). Per-Region pricing varies. Inter-Region traffic is billable. PRIOR VERSION HAD WRONG CORRECT-ANSWER INDEX (marked a factually false claim about default cross-Region replication) — fixed 2026-05-13.

questions.q: AWS infrastructure inside one Region is partitioned into multiple physically isolated facility groups, each with its OWN power, cooling, and network — connected to each other by sub-ms private fibre. A Region typically has 3+ of these. What's the AWS term for one of these facility groups?
choices: Availability Zone (AZ) — one or more discrete data-centre facilities with independent power, cooling, and network inside a single Region, connected by low-latency links
Region — the geographic AREA that CONTAINS the AZs; one level above the per-AZ facility group described in the question's scope of physical isolation
Edge Location / CloudFront POP — global edge cache footprint outside the Region's data centres; not the Region-internal isolated facility group
VPC subnet — a customer-defined logical network primitive inside a Region; not the AWS-managed physical-facility unit described in the question
questions.explanation: An AZ is one or more data centers within a Region with independent power, cooling, and networking. Multiple AZs in a Region enable high availability architecture.

questions.q: A cloud-101 lecture defines a property as: 'resources can be ADDED or REMOVED automatically in response to demand signals, and you pay only for actual usage'. This contrasts with the on-prem paradigm of static, over-provisioned peak capacity. Which cloud property is this?
choices: Manual capacity stretching of on-prem hardware bought ahead of demand — not elasticity, which automatically adjusts capacity in response to demand signals
Automatic scaling up AND down with demand, paying for actual usage — the textbook elasticity property of the cloud, opposite of static fixed allocation
Annual long-horizon capacity planning with a fixed reserved allocation up front — opposite of dynamic elasticity that automatically adjusts capacity to demand
Static fixed allocation reserved for peak load even when demand is low — the on-prem model that elasticity replaces with dynamic auto-scale-up and scale-down
questions.explanation: Elasticity = dynamically scale resources with demand + pay for actual usage. PRIOR VERSION HAD WRONG CORRECT-ANSWER INDEX (marked static peak allocation as elasticity, which is exactly backwards) — fixed 2026-05-13.

questions.q: An auditor asks AWS who is responsible for: (1) the physical security of the data centre, (2) hypervisor patching, (3) the customer's EC2 guest OS patching, (4) the customer's application data encryption. Which mapping is correct under the Shared Responsibility Model?
choices: Customer owns ALL four items — incorrect; AWS owns the security of the cloud foundation including datacentre, hardware, hypervisor, and network
AWS owns ALL four items — incorrect; customers own security IN the cloud, including guest OS patching, IAM, data, and application configuration
Mapping varies by support tier — incorrect; the shared-responsibility model is fixed and not influenced by which support tier the account holds
AWS = security OF the cloud (DC, hardware, hypervisor, network); Customer = security IN the cloud (guest OS, IAM, data, application configuration)
questions.explanation: AWS: physical security, data center facilities, networking hardware, hypervisor, and managed service infrastructure. Customer: everything they put in the cloud — data encryption, IAM, OS patching on EC2, network config.

questions.q: An architect designing for high availability must distinguish two AWS scope concepts: (1) a geographic area containing multiple isolated data-centre clusters connected by low-latency fibre, (2) one or more of those data-centre clusters in distinct power/cooling/network failure domains. Which mapping is correct?
choices: Both are interchangeable labels for the same physical datacentre; AZs are server racks inside the Region's datacentre with shared power, cooling, and network feeds
A Region is a geographic area containing multiple isolated Availability Zones; each Availability Zone is one or more physically separated datacentres with independent power and network
A Region is a load-balancer pool and an Availability Zone is the IP subnet associated with that pool inside a virtual private cloud network in the customer's account
A Region is a marketing label only, with no physical separation between Availability Zones inside it; all zones share the same power and network feeds in this view
questions.explanation: A Region (e.g., us-east-1) is a geographic cluster of AZs. An AZ (e.g., us-east-1a) is one or more data centers with independent infrastructure. Multi-AZ deployments protect against single data center failure.

questions.q: Under the Shared Responsibility Model, for a Lambda function deployed in customer code, who is responsible for: (a) hypervisor patching, (b) Lambda runtime (e.g., python3.12) patching, (c) the customer's function CODE, (d) the IAM role attached, (e) the data the function reads/writes?
choices: Customer owns the runtime and underlying OS — false; AWS owns the Lambda runtime and the underlying operating system patching responsibilities entirely
Customer handles only OS patching — false; AWS handles operating-system patching for the Lambda execution environment and the runtime updates themselves
Identical to EC2 — false; Lambda is more managed than EC2, so customers own less of the stack and AWS handles the OS and runtime patching entirely
AWS handles infrastructure, OS, and runtime patching; customer handles the function code, IAM role configuration, business data, and runtime configuration values
questions.explanation: Serverless shifts more responsibility to AWS. For Lambda, you don't manage: servers, OS, runtime patches, capacity. You still own: your code, IAM roles, data encryption, network access, and application-level security.

questions.q: A workload in a single AZ is taken offline when that AZ has a utility-power incident. The architect spreads the workload across 3 AZs in the same Region. Why does this design eliminate the single-AZ failure?
choices: AZs are labels for the same datacentre with no real physical isolation — false; AZs are physically separate facilities with independent power and network
AZs share power, cooling, and network feeds across the entire region — false; each AZ has independent power, cooling, and network feeds inside the region
AZs are physically separate facilities with independent power, cooling, and network; spreading workloads across three AZs survives single-AZ failure
Multi-AZ deployments double the cost regardless of architecture across every service — generic false; multi-AZ cost varies by service and configuration
questions.explanation: Each AZ is one or more discrete data centers with redundant power/network. They're connected with low-latency links but isolated from each other's failures. Multi-AZ = high availability. ELB + Auto Scaling + RDS Multi-AZ = HA architecture.

nodes.title: Storage concepts: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Cloud storage comes in three flavors with very different cost/perf trade-offs: object (think S3), block (think EBS / managed disks), and file (think EFS / Azure Files / Filestore). Pick wrong and you either overpay or hit performance ceilings.

flashcards.front: Object vs block vs file storage — when do you use each?
flashcards.back: Object (S3, Blob, GCS) for unstructured data, backups, static sites, data lakes — flat namespace, HTTP API, infinite scale. Block (EBS, managed disks) for OS disks and databases — low latency, single attach. File (EFS, NFS) when multiple VMs need a shared POSIX filesystem.

flashcards.front: What is a storage class / tier?
flashcards.back: Same data, different SLA and price. Hot tier (frequent access, expensive read, cheap retrieval). Cold/archive tier (rare access, cheap to store, expensive to read, retrieval latency from minutes to hours). Lifecycle policies move data between tiers automatically.

flashcards.front: Why use server-side encryption?
flashcards.back: Data is encrypted at rest by the storage service using either provider-managed keys (default, no extra config) or your own keys via KMS. This protects against physical disk theft and meets compliance baselines without changing your app code.

flashcards.front: What's storage durability vs availability?
flashcards.back: Durability is the chance your data won't be lost (object stores claim ~11 9s — 99.999999999%). Availability is the chance you can reach it right now (typically 4 9s — 99.99%). Durability is multi-region replication; availability is how many concurrent failures the service tolerates.

questions.q: A team needs durable OBJECT storage for any size of file, REST-API-accessible, with 99.999999999% (11 nines) durability and globally addressable URLs. They don't need a POSIX filesystem. Which AWS service?
choices: Amazon EBS — block storage attached to a single EC2 instance, with POSIX semantics and no object-style HTTPS URL access at internet scale
Amazon S3 — object storage with 11-nines durability, HTTPS REST access, virtually unlimited scale, and globally addressable bucket-and-key URLs
Amazon EFS — managed POSIX NFS file system shared across many EC2 instances, with directory semantics rather than object-style HTTPS access
EC2 Instance Store — ephemeral local SSD attached to the host, lost on stop, with no managed durability, scale, or REST access guarantees
questions.explanation: Amazon S3 (Simple Storage Service) is AWS's object storage service. It stores data as objects in buckets, offers 99.999999999% (11 9s) durability.

questions.q: A team has medical imaging files that are accessed about 4× per year but, when accessed, must be retrievable in MILLISECONDS (not hours). They want to pay less than S3 Standard storage rates. Which S3 storage class fits?
choices: S3 Standard-IA — same millisecond retrieval as Standard at a lower per-GB storage rate with a per-GB retrieval fee; designed for infrequent-access objects like the medical images
S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval — minutes-to-hours retrieval times; cheaper storage but does not meet the millisecond-retrieval requirement for the medical imaging files
S3 Standard — millisecond retrieval and lowest retrieval cost but the most expensive per-GB storage tier; ill-suited for the infrequent-access pattern described
S3 Glacier Deep Archive — hours-long retrieval and the cheapest storage; not a millisecond-retrieval tier for the medical imaging files described
questions.explanation: S3 Standard-IA is for data accessed less frequently but needs immediate access when required. Lower storage cost than S3 Standard but retrieval fee applies.

questions.q: A relational database on EC2 needs PERSISTENT block storage that survives instance stop/start AND can be reattached to a different instance in the same AZ. The storage must be a /dev/sdX block device the OS formats with a filesystem. Which AWS storage primitive fits?
choices: Amazon S3 — durable object storage with an HTTPS REST API; not a block device that an EC2 instance can attach as /dev/xvdb and mount with a filesystem
Amazon EBS — persistent block storage volume that outlives the instance, can be detached and reattached, and is presented as /dev/xvd*
Amazon EFS — managed POSIX NFS file system shared across instances; not a block device attached as /dev/xvdb with its own filesystem
EC2 Instance Store — ephemeral local SSD attached to the host; data is lost on stop or terminate and cannot be reattached to another instance
questions.explanation: EBS (Elastic Block Store) provides persistent block storage volumes attached to EC2. Unlike instance store, EBS persists after instance stop/terminate and can be detached/reattached.

questions.q: A fleet of 12 EC2 web servers in 3 AZs must SHARE one writable filesystem so user uploads written by one server are immediately visible to the others. The filesystem must be POSIX with NFS-mount semantics, scale storage automatically, and be regional (multi-AZ). Which AWS service?
choices: Amazon EFS — elastic NFS file system that mounts across many EC2 instances simultaneously and spans multiple AZs; POSIX-compliant shared writable filesystem
Amazon EBS — single-instance block volume; multi-attach is limited to a few enterprise-class volumes and is not a multi-AZ NFS-style shared filesystem
Amazon S3 — durable object storage with an HTTPS REST API; not a POSIX filesystem that mounts on many EC2 instances with NFS-style concurrent semantics
AWS Storage Gateway tape archive — virtual tape library for backup workflows; not a POSIX shared filesystem that mounts on many EC2 instances simultaneously
questions.explanation: EFS (Elastic File System) is a managed NFS file system that can be mounted to multiple EC2 instances across Availability Zones simultaneously. Unlike EBS which attaches to one instance.

questions.q: A bucket holding critical compliance docs is at risk of accidental overwrite/delete by the application or by an admin. The team wants to retain a HISTORY of every object version, recover prior versions, and undelete tombstoned objects. Which S3 feature?
choices: Bucket-creation order counter — not a real S3 feature; there is no per-bucket counter that retains object version history or supports recovery
Bucket-policy history — would track IAM-policy changes if it existed; does not retain a history of every object version and supports no rollback
S3 Versioning — retains every version of every object; PUT and DELETE create new versions or delete markers, enabling recovery of accidentally lost data
S3 Object-level CloudTrail — audits API calls against objects but does not retain object content, so it cannot recover overwritten or deleted bytes
questions.explanation: S3 Versioning stores all versions of an object including writes and deletes. Enables recovery from accidental overwrites/deletes. Can be used with Lifecycle policies to manage costs.

questions.q: A compliance archive of CT scan images must be retained 30 years. Access frequency is well below 1 read per year. Retrieval latency may be 12 hours. Minimum storage cost is the only optimisation criterion. Which S3 storage class fits?
choices: S3 Glacier Deep Archive — lowest per-GB cost, multi-hour retrieval, ideal for 30-yr cold archive
S3 Standard — most expensive per GB, ms retrieval, wrong for sub-yearly access
S3 Intelligent-Tiering — auto-tiers based on access; the access pattern here puts it into archive tiers ANYWAY at additional management fee
S3 One Zone-IA — single-AZ infrequent access, higher per-GB than Deep Archive
questions.explanation: S3 storage classes by access frequency: Standard > Intelligent-Tiering > Standard-IA > One Zone-IA > Glacier Instant > Glacier Flexible Retrieval > Glacier Deep Archive. Match access pattern to class to minimize costs.

questions.q: A team needs MANAGED file systems for specific protocols: SMB for Windows file shares, Lustre for high-performance computing, NetApp ONTAP for migration from on-prem ONTAP, OpenZFS for ZFS workloads. They want one AWS service family that covers all four. Which?
choices: A new EBS volume type — block-storage volume attached to a single EC2 instance; not a managed file-system family covering SMB, Lustre, NetApp ONTAP, or OpenZFS
Amazon FSx (FSx for Windows / Lustre / NetApp ONTAP / OpenZFS) — managed file-system family that covers each of those protocols and engines under one name
Amazon EFS — managed NFS file system only; does not cover SMB for Windows, Lustre for HPC, NetApp ONTAP, or OpenZFS file-system protocols and engines
AWS Storage Gateway — exposes S3 as on-prem file shares and tapes via a gateway appliance; a different surface than the managed file-system family above
questions.explanation: FSx is the managed file-systems family: Windows File Server (SMB), Lustre (HPC), NetApp ONTAP, OpenZFS. Storage Gateway is different (hybrid). PRIOR VERSION HAD WRONG CORRECT-ANSWER INDEX (marked Storage Gateway as the FSx definition) — fixed 2026-05-13.

nodes.title: Compute services: Key Ideas
nodes.content: 'Compute' is everything that runs your code: VMs, containers, serverless functions, batch jobs. The exam wants you to pick the right shape — long-running stateful workload → VM, packaged app → container, event-driven short job → serverless.

flashcards.front: VM vs container vs serverless — pick a service for each.
flashcards.back: VM (EC2 / Compute Engine / Azure VM) when you need full OS control. Container (ECS, GKE, AKS, Cloud Run) when you've packaged an app and want orchestration. Serverless (Lambda, Functions, Cloud Functions) for short event-driven tasks, no infrastructure to manage.

flashcards.front: What is autoscaling?
flashcards.back: A service that adds/removes compute instances based on a signal (CPU, request rate, queue depth, custom metric). Scale-out is cheap; scale-in saves money. Target tracking is the simplest mode: 'keep average CPU at 60%'.

flashcards.front: Spot / preemptible / low-priority — what's the catch?
flashcards.back: Up to 90% off list price, but the cloud can yank the instance with 30 s – 2 min warning. Use for fault-tolerant batch jobs, CI runners, big-data clusters. Don't use for stateful databases or anything that needs to stay up.

flashcards.front: Reserved / committed-use vs on-demand pricing.
flashcards.back: On-demand: pay by the hour or second, no commitment. Reserved / committed: 1-3 year commitment, 30-60% discount, no flexibility. Pick reserved for steady baseline load, on-demand for spiky workloads.

questions.q: A developer needs to run a Python function in response to S3 object-creation events with NO server to provision, NO OS to patch, billing in 1 ms increments only when the function runs. Which AWS service fits?
choices: AWS Lambda — serverless function-as-a-service: event-driven, no infra, per-ms billing, ≤15 min execution
Amazon EC2 — VMs that the customer must provision, patch, and pay for hourly while idle
Amazon ECS — container orchestrator that still needs the customer to manage container infra (or run on Fargate)
Amazon Lightsail — bundled small-VM offering, still customer-managed instances
questions.explanation: AWS Lambda is a serverless compute service. You upload code and Lambda runs it in response to events. You pay only for execution time — no server management required.

questions.q: A web tier sized for steady traffic gets bursty afternoon spikes. The team wants the fleet to GROW to absorb peak and SHRINK when demand drops, automatically based on CPU and request-count metrics, without operator intervention. Which AWS feature?
choices: EC2 instance-family swap — manual right-sizing performed on each instance; not a dynamic capacity-add/remove mechanism driven by CPU and request signals
Automated OS patching — operational hygiene that keeps the fleet secure; it does not grow or shrink fleet capacity in response to demand
AWS Auto Scaling (EC2 Auto Scaling Groups + scaling policies) — automatically adds or removes instances based on demand signals such as CPU and request load
Scheduled RDS / EBS backups — backup operations on databases and volumes; they do not grow or shrink the EC2 fleet based on application demand
questions.explanation: AWS Auto Scaling monitors applications and automatically adjusts capacity (EC2 instances, ECS tasks, etc.) to maintain performance and minimize costs.

questions.q: A web tier has 6 EC2 instances serving HTTPS. A new release introduces autoscaling — at peak the fleet may grow to 30, at trough shrink to 3. The team needs a managed service that automatically registers/deregisters scaling instances and distributes inbound HTTPS requests with health checks. Which AWS service?
choices: Amazon CloudFront — edge CDN for cached content, not a back-end load distributor
Amazon RDS read-replica — database scaling, not HTTPS distribution
Amazon Route 53 weighted records — DNS-level distribution, no per-request layer-7 health checking like ELB
Elastic Load Balancing — distributes inbound to EC2 / containers / IP / Lambda targets with health checks
questions.explanation: ELB distributes traffic across multiple targets. ALB (Application) = Layer 7/HTTP, NLB (Network) = Layer 4/TCP, GLB (Gateway) = Layer 3 for third-party appliances. Integrates with Auto Scaling.

questions.q: A small dev team wants to deploy a Node.js web app to AWS without configuring the underlying EC2 / LB / autoscaling / health-checks themselves. They upload the source, AWS provisions everything based on the platform, scales it, and updates it. Which AWS service fits?
choices: Amazon EKS — managed Kubernetes control plane; the team still owns workloads, container definitions, and scaling configuration rather than receiving a turnkey PaaS
Amazon ECR — managed container image registry only; not a PaaS that provisions EC2, load balancer, autoscaling, and health checks behind a simple deploy
AWS CDK — Infrastructure-as-Code tool that synthesises CloudFormation from imperative code; a provisioning tool, not a runtime PaaS that auto-manages all of that
AWS Elastic Beanstalk — PaaS that provisions EC2, load balancer, autoscaling, and health checks behind a simple application deploy with rolling updates and rollbacks
questions.explanation: Elastic Beanstalk is a PaaS that deploys web apps (Java, .NET, PHP, Node.js, Python, Ruby, Go, Docker). You upload code; Beanstalk handles the infrastructure. You still control the underlying resources.

questions.q: A backend must orchestrate this flow: (1) start a Lambda, (2) wait for human approval, (3) run a Glue ETL job, (4) on success notify SNS, (5) on failure invoke a different Lambda. The flow is long-running, has retries with exponential backoff, and is auditable. Which service?
choices: AWS Lambda chained directly with synchronous invocations only — possible but lacks built-in state tracking, automatic retries, and visual workflow representation for the steps
Amazon SQS alone — provides reliable queueing primitives but no built-in orchestration, branching, or visual representation of multi-step workflow logic
AWS Step Functions — managed state-machine workflow orchestrator with built-in retries, branching, parallelism, and a visual graph of the multi-step Lambda chain
Amazon EventBridge alone — event bus that routes events between services but offers no built-in retries, branching, or visual orchestration of a multi-step workflow
questions.explanation: Step Functions orchestrates distributed applications as state machines with visual workflows. Coordinates Lambda, ECS, DynamoDB, SNS, SQS, and more with built-in error handling and retries.

questions.q: A pre-baked OS image with a specific Linux distro, kernel version, pre-installed nginx + Python venv, and security-hardened config is published as a reusable EC2 image. Launching a new EC2 from this image gives you that EXACT environment. What is this template called?
choices: AWS Management Console — browser-based admin UI for AWS; not the pre-baked OS image template used to launch EC2 instances with pre-installed software
An Amazon Machine Image (AMI) — template (root volume snapshot + launch permissions + block-device mapping) that EC2 uses to provision new instances
An asymmetric key-pair — used to SSH into a Linux instance after launch; not the OS-image template used to launch EC2 instances with pre-installed software
A VPC template — defines a virtual network (CIDR, subnets, route tables); not the OS-image template used to launch EC2 instances with pre-installed software
questions.explanation: An AMI is the EC2 launch template: it bundles a root volume snapshot, launch permissions, and a block-device mapping. AMI ≠ the browser management console. PRIOR VERSION HAD WRONG CORRECT-ANSWER INDEX — fixed 2026-05-13.

questions.q: A first Lambda invocation after a long idle period shows 800 ms of added latency. The next invocation a second later finishes in 30 ms. The 800-ms first-hit overhead is documented as the time to provision a new execution environment, download the deployment package, start the runtime, and run any module-level init. Which Lambda phenomenon is this?
choices: Region cold start — would be a one-time event spanning all regional invocations; not the per-execution-environment latency the question describes for a Lambda function
Billing first-invocation surcharge — not a real Lambda billing item; Lambda bills per request and per GB-second, with no separate first-invocation surcharge
Cold start — execution-environment provisioning, runtime load, and customer init code (typically 100 ms - 1 s) added to the first invocation after idle
Execution timeout — happens at the END of a too-long invocation; not the start-up latency added to the first invocation after a long idle period
questions.explanation: Lambda cold start = time to provision container + load runtime + init your code. Mitigation: Provisioned Concurrency (keeps environments warm), Lambda SnapStart (Java), smaller deployment packages, faster runtimes (Node/Python vs Java).

nodes.title: Cloud governance: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Governance is the set of policies and guardrails that keep a cloud account safe and on-budget as it scales from one engineer to a hundred. Think tagging standards, budget alerts, organizational policies, and the multi-account strategy.

flashcards.front: Why use multiple accounts (an Organization) instead of one big account?
flashcards.back: Blast-radius isolation: a compromised prod account doesn't leak into dev. Billing clarity: per-team or per-environment cost reports. Quota independence: prod doesn't share API limits with sandbox. Service Control Policies (AWS) / management groups (Azure) enforce 'no one can disable CloudTrail' across the whole org.

flashcards.front: What is a Service Control Policy (SCP)?
flashcards.back: An AWS Organizations policy that sets the maximum permissions any IAM identity in a member account can have. Even if a user's IAM policy grants `s3:*`, an SCP denying `s3:DeleteBucket` overrides it. SCPs are guardrails, not grants — they only restrict.

flashcards.front: Tagging strategy — name three high-leverage tags.
flashcards.back: (1) Owner / team — who pays and who to page. (2) Environment (prod/staging/dev) — drives access controls and lifecycle. (3) Cost-center / project — for chargeback. Tags are free and infinitely valuable for cost allocation and automation; enforce them with policies.

flashcards.front: What is a landing zone?
flashcards.back: A pre-baked multi-account setup with security baselines: org with master + audit + log-archive + workload accounts, CloudTrail / Config enabled everywhere, SSO wired up, network templates ready. AWS Control Tower / Azure Landing Zones / GCP setup automate this so you start on a safe foundation, not bare cloud.

questions.q: An ops team wants automated recommendations across COST (idle resources, RI coverage), PERFORMANCE (under-provisioned instances), SECURITY (open SGs, root MFA), FAULT TOLERANCE (no Multi-AZ), and SERVICE LIMITS (approaching quotas) — refreshed continuously and surfaced in the console. Which AWS service?
choices: External pen-test firm — manual engagement focused on offensive security findings; not a continuous AWS service emitting automated recommendations
AWS IAM Access Analyzer — narrower analysis of resource-based policies for external sharing; not the broad five-pillar automated recommendation engine
AWS Organizations — multi-account governance with OUs, SCPs, and consolidated billing; not a service-level automated recommendation engine across pillars
AWS Trusted Advisor — automated checks across five pillars (cost, performance, security, fault tolerance, service limits) with actionable recommendations
questions.explanation: Trusted Advisor inspects your AWS environment and provides actionable recommendations. Basic checks (free): S3 bucket permissions, MFA on root account. Full checks require Business or Enterprise support.

questions.q: A compliance team needs the AWS service that: (a) takes a snapshot of every resource's CONFIGURATION over time, (b) evaluates each snapshot against rules (e.g., 'S3 bucket must have versioning enabled'), (c) surfaces drift with timeline + non-compliant flag. Which service?
choices: AWS Systems Manager — manages running EC2 (patching, sessions), not RM-config history
AWS Config — records resource configuration history and evaluates against rules
AWS CodeDeploy — deploys application code to EC2 / on-prem / Lambda; not config recording
AWS IAM Access Analyzer — analyses IAM grants, not resource config history
questions.explanation: AWS Config is the configuration-recording / rule-evaluation service. CodeDeploy deploys application code. Systems Manager is run-time admin. PRIOR VERSION HAD WRONG CORRECT-ANSWER INDEX (marked CodeDeploy's description as Config) — fixed 2026-05-13.

questions.q: A company has 40+ AWS accounts. They want one place to: (a) create new accounts, (b) cluster them into OUs, (c) apply guardrails via Service Control Policies, (d) consolidate billing into one invoice. Which AWS service?
choices: AWS IAM Identity Center — workforce SSO and permission-set assignment across multiple AWS accounts; not the multi-account governance plane with OUs, SCPs, and billing
AWS Migration Hub — tracks application migrations across AWS tools; not the multi-account governance plane with OUs, Service Control Policies, and consolidated billing
AWS Organizations — central multi-account management plane with OUs, Service Control Policies, consolidated billing, and Account Factory for new accounts
AWS Auto Scaling — coordinates dynamic capacity scaling across multiple AWS services; not the multi-account governance plane with OUs, SCPs, and consolidated billing
questions.explanation: AWS Organizations enables centralized management of multiple AWS accounts: consolidated billing (volume discounts), Service Control Policies to restrict account permissions, and account grouping in OUs.

questions.q: Inside AWS Organizations, a permission GUARDRAIL applies at the OU or account level. It can DENY (or filter) what any IAM principal — including the account's root user — is allowed to do. It does NOT grant permissions, only caps them. Which construct is this?
choices: An IAM identity-based policy attached to users / groups / roles — grants permissions, not a guardrail cap
A Service Control Policy (SCP) at the OU or account scope — the GUARDRAIL that caps maximum permissions
A VPC-level network policy filtering subnet traffic — networking, not IAM
A CloudFormation template that provisions stacks — IaC, not a permission guardrail
questions.explanation: SCPs are the AWS Organizations guardrail: they cap (deny / filter) the maximum permissions for IAM principals in the targeted OU / account, including the account's root user. They never GRANT — they only restrict. PRIOR VERSION HAD WRONG CORRECT-ANSWER INDEX (marked CloudFormation, which is IaC) — fixed 2026-05-13.

questions.q: An architect new to AWS asks where to find AWS's prescriptive best-practice guidance, organised into pillars that an architecture review can score against (with detailed lenses for serverless, machine-learning, SaaS, IoT). Which official AWS resource is this?
choices: AWS Marketplace — catalogue of third-party software and SaaS listings for purchase; it does not host AWS's prescriptive best-practice pillars or framework guidance
AWS Well-Architected Framework — six pillars (operational excellence, security, reliability, performance, cost, sustainability) plus domain-specific lenses with prescriptive best-practice guidance
AWS Service Catalog — lets internal admins curate approved CloudFormation templates for end users; it does not host AWS's prescriptive best-practice pillars or framework guidance
AWS Solutions Library — pre-built reference implementations for common workloads; useful examples, but not the canonical place for AWS's prescriptive best-practice pillars and lenses
questions.explanation: The Well-Architected Framework helps architects build secure, high-performing, resilient, and efficient infrastructure. Use the Well-Architected Tool in the AWS console for free architectural reviews.

questions.q: A company has Oracle, SQL Server, and Windows Server licences they own (BYOL). They want a managed inventory tool that tracks each license, attaches them to AWS / on-prem instances, and alerts when a deployment would exceed the licence count. Which AWS service?
choices: AWS License Manager — manages BYOL licences across AWS and on-prem fleets, enforces seat limits, attaches them to instances, and generates compliance reports
AWS Marketplace — catalogue for buying third-party AMIs and SaaS subscriptions; not a BYOL-license inventory and enforcement engine across AWS and on-prem
AWS Cost Explorer — visualises spend trends and forecast across accounts and services; not a BYOL-license inventory and enforcement engine across AWS and on-prem
AWS Resource Groups — groups arbitrary AWS resources by tag for batch operations; not a BYOL-license inventory and enforcement engine across AWS and on-prem
questions.explanation: License Manager helps track BYOL (Bring Your Own License) software deployments on EC2, prevents launching instances that would violate license terms, and provides a centralized dashboard for license inventory.

questions.q: An enterprise wants AWS to set up a multi-account 'landing zone' for them — pre-baked OUs, guardrails enforced via SCPs, a 'log archive' account, an 'audit' account, an Account Factory for new accounts. They want this in a few clicks, not via custom CloudFormation. Which AWS service?
choices: AWS Data Center Inventory — not a real AWS service; no canonical AWS product by this label sets up a multi-account landing zone with OUs and guardrails
AWS Artifact — self-service portal for AWS compliance reports; does not set up a multi-account landing zone with OUs, SCP guardrails, or Account Factory
AWS IAM role lifecycle manager — not a real AWS service; no canonical AWS product by this label sets up a multi-account landing zone with OUs and guardrails
AWS Control Tower — automates a multi-account Landing Zone with pre-baked OUs, SCP guardrails, log-archive and audit accounts, and Account Factory provisioning
questions.explanation: Control Tower builds a Landing Zone with: Log Archive account, Audit account, and an Account Factory. Guardrails (preventive = SCPs, detective = Config Rules) enforce compliance automatically across all accounts.

nodes.title: AWS analytics services: Key Ideas
nodes.content: AWS offers a suite of managed analytics services covering data warehousing, stream processing, interactive querying, and BI. The Cloud Practitioner exam tests which service to use for each scenario.

flashcards.front: Amazon Redshift — primary use case?
flashcards.back: Columnar data warehouse for petabyte-scale SQL analytics on structured data; not for OLTP or real-time streaming.

flashcards.front: Amazon Kinesis vs SQS — when to choose Kinesis?
flashcards.back: Kinesis for real-time ordered streaming with multiple consumers and replay; SQS for decoupled task queues with at-least-once delivery.

flashcards.front: Amazon Athena — how does it query data?
flashcards.back: Serverless interactive SQL on data stored in S3; no infrastructure to manage, pay per query (per TB scanned).

flashcards.front: AWS Glue role in an analytics pipeline?
flashcards.back: Managed ETL service: crawls data sources to build a Data Catalog, then runs serverless Spark jobs to transform and load data.

questions.q: An analytics team runs SQL queries over 500 TB of clickstream data. The workload is read-heavy, scans large columns of a few facts at a time, joins to dimension tables, and benefits from columnar compression + MPP (massively parallel processing). Which AWS service?
choices: ElastiCache — in-memory key-value cache for sub-millisecond reads; not a petabyte-scale columnar warehouse with MPP for SQL analytics over facts and dimensions
RDS for MySQL/PostgreSQL — managed OLTP relational database; not a petabyte-scale columnar warehouse with MPP for SQL analytics over facts and dimensions
Amazon Redshift — managed columnar data warehouse with massively parallel processing and Spectrum-to-S3 for petabyte-scale SQL analytics over facts and dimensions
DynamoDB — managed NoSQL key-value and document store; not a petabyte-scale columnar warehouse with MPP for SQL analytics over facts and dimensions
questions.explanation: Redshift is AWS's managed data warehouse for analytics (OLAP). Uses columnar storage and MPP (Massively Parallel Processing) to run complex analytical queries across petabytes of data.

questions.q: A telemetry pipeline must ingest 1 million events/sec from IoT devices, retain them ordered for 24-168 hours, and let multiple consumers replay the stream (Lambda, Firehose to S3, Analytics with windowing). Which AWS service is the streaming primitive?
choices: Amazon RDS — managed relational database; not a streaming primitive that retains ordered events for hours across shards with multiple replay consumers
Amazon Kinesis Data Streams — managed, shard-partitioned, ordered event stream with multiple consumers and 24-168 hour retention for replay
Amazon S3 — durable object store that can act as a Kinesis SINK via Firehose; not the streaming primitive itself that ingests and replays ordered events
Amazon SQS — pull-based message queue with visibility timeout and delete semantics; not the streaming ordered-replayable model the pipeline requires
questions.explanation: Kinesis Data Streams is the streaming primitive: shard-partitioned, ordered within a shard, retention 24-168 hours, multiple consumers can replay. PRIOR VERSION HAD WRONG CORRECT-ANSWER INDEX (marked RDS as the streaming answer) — fixed 2026-05-13.

questions.q: A team wants to run ad-hoc SQL queries DIRECTLY against parquet/CSV/JSON files stored in S3, with NO database to provision, billed per TB scanned. Which AWS service?
choices: Amazon RDS — managed relational database; data must be loaded into engine tables first, not queried in-place against parquet/CSV/JSON files sitting on S3
Amazon Athena — serverless interactive SQL directly over parquet/CSV/JSON files on S3, billed per TB scanned, with no provisioned infrastructure to manage
AWS Database Migration Service (DMS) — moves databases between engines and into AWS; not an in-place SQL engine over parquet/CSV/JSON files on S3
AWS Glue — managed ETL service; its Data Catalog feeds Athena, but Glue itself is not the interactive query engine over parquet/CSV/JSON files on S3
questions.explanation: Athena is serverless ANSI SQL over data in S3 using Presto/Trino. Billed per TB scanned. Uses the Glue Data Catalog. DMS is a migration tool. PRIOR VERSION HAD WRONG CORRECT-ANSWER INDEX — fixed 2026-05-13.

questions.q: A team wants a managed ETL service to (a) crawl source data, build a data catalog with schemas, (b) author and run Spark / Python jobs that transform S3 / RDS / Redshift data, (c) all serverless. Which AWS service?
choices: VPC Reachability Analyzer — networking diagnostic, unrelated
AWS CodePipeline — CI/CD pipeline, not data ETL
AWS Glue — serverless ETL with Crawlers + Data Catalog + Spark/Python jobs
Amazon Kinesis Data Streams — real-time streaming primitive, not batch ETL with a catalog
questions.explanation: AWS Glue provides: Data Catalog (metadata repository for all your data sources), ETL jobs (serverless Spark-based transformations), and Crawlers (auto-discover schema from S3, RDS, etc.).

questions.q: Finance asks BI for monthly KPI dashboards over Athena/Redshift/RDS data, accessible in a browser, no servers to operate, with per-reader pricing. Which AWS service fits?
choices: Amazon CloudWatch — operational-metrics dashboards over AWS infrastructure metrics; not a BI tool over Athena, Redshift, or RDS data with per-reader pricing
Amazon QuickSight — serverless BI service with dashboards over S3 / Redshift / Athena / RDS / databases and per-reader pricing for end-user consumption
AWS Glue — managed ETL service for cataloguing and transforming data; does not render BI dashboards over Athena, Redshift, or RDS for finance users
AWS CloudTrail — control-plane audit logs of AWS API calls; not a BI dashboard tool over Athena, Redshift, or RDS data with per-reader pricing
questions.explanation: QuickSight connects to dozens of data sources and enables self-service BI with SPICE (in-memory computation engine). ML Insights adds anomaly detection and forecasting. Pay-per-session pricing model.

nodes.title: AWS cost management: Key Ideas
nodes.content: AWS provides several tools to monitor, forecast, and reduce spending. The Cloud Practitioner exam asks which tool to use for billing analysis, budgets, and rightsizing recommendations.

flashcards.front: AWS Cost Explorer vs AWS Budgets?
flashcards.back: Cost Explorer: visualise and analyse past and forecasted spend. AWS Budgets: set spend/usage thresholds and receive alerts when approaching them.

flashcards.front: What does AWS Trusted Advisor's cost pillar check?
flashcards.back: Identifies idle or underutilised resources (e.g., low-CPU EC2, unattached EBS), Reserved Instance optimisation, and savings plan coverage gaps.

flashcards.front: Three ways to reduce AWS compute costs?
flashcards.back: Reserved Instances (1–3 yr commitment, up to 72% off), Savings Plans (flexible compute discount), and Spot Instances (spare capacity, up to 90% off).

flashcards.front: AWS Cost Allocation Tags — purpose?
flashcards.back: User-defined key-value pairs on resources; activate in Billing Console to break down costs by team, project, or environment in Cost Explorer.

questions.q: An architect needs to estimate the MONTHLY cost of a planned deployment (10 EC2 m6i.xlarge + 5 TB S3 Standard + 1 RDS db.m5.large + 100 GB data transfer) BEFORE provisioning anything. Which AWS tool produces a per-service estimate from the catalogue pricing?
choices: AWS Cost Explorer — analyses already-incurred costs by service, tag, and account over time; not a pre-deployment monthly estimate of a planned new deployment
AWS Pricing Calculator — public web tool for estimating monthly cost from catalogue list prices before deploying anything, including EC2, RDS, S3, and data transfer
AWS Budgets — alerts on real or forecast spend versus a threshold for an account or tag; not a pre-deployment monthly estimate of a planned new deployment
AWS Trusted Advisor — best-practice recommendations on running infrastructure across cost, performance, security, and reliability; not a pre-deployment monthly estimate
questions.explanation: The AWS Pricing Calculator lets you estimate monthly costs for AWS services before you deploy them. Cost Explorer analyzes existing costs; Budgets sets alerts.

questions.q: A FinOps analyst wants to (a) chart historical spend per service / per tag / per linked account, (b) compare last quarter to this, (c) drill into cost spikes. The analysis is over ALREADY-INCURRED costs, not estimates. Which AWS service?
choices: AWS Pricing Calculator — free pre-deploy estimation tool for a proposed architecture; not a deep historical drill-down over actual past spend per service and tag
AWS Budgets — sets cost and usage budgets with email or SNS alerts when actual or forecast spend crosses a threshold; not a deep historical drill-down chart
AWS Cost Explorer — visualises and analyses actual AWS cost and usage history with grouping by service, tag, account, and time range, with drill-down on spikes
AWS Artifact — self-service portal for AWS compliance reports such as SOC and PCI; not a deep historical drill-down chart over AWS cost and usage history
questions.explanation: Cost Explorer lets you analyze historical cost trends, identify cost drivers, forecast future spend, and find optimization opportunities with detailed filtering and charting.

questions.q: A finance team wants to be alerted when AWS spend hits 50%, 80%, and 100% of the monthly budget. The control must also support automatic actions (e.g., stop EC2 instances, apply an IAM policy) on threshold breach. Which AWS service?
choices: AWS Cost Explorer alerts only — provides historical and forecast charts but cannot directly trigger budget-driven email or automated stop-EC2 actions at thresholds
AWS Budgets — set monthly cost or usage budgets at 50/80/100% thresholds with email/SNS alerts and optional Budget Actions to stop EC2 or apply an IAM policy
AWS Trusted Advisor budget module — surfaces cost-optimisation checks but does not directly emit threshold alerts at 50/80/100% or apply policy actions
Amazon CloudWatch metric alarms only — fires on metrics like CPU; supports custom cost metrics but is not the canonical AWS service for monthly cost budgets and actions
questions.explanation: AWS Budgets lets you define cost/usage/RI coverage budgets with SNS email/SMS alerts. Budget Actions can automatically apply IAM policies or stop EC2/RDS instances when thresholds are crossed.

questions.q: An architect needs to forecast the monthly cost of a PROPOSED architecture (Lambda + DynamoDB + S3 + CloudFront + Route 53) BEFORE deploying anything. The tool must use AWS list prices and produce a per-service breakdown. Which AWS tool?
choices: AWS Bills — shows past spend by account, service, and tag; useful for after-the-fact analysis but not for forecasting a not-yet-deployed proposed architecture
AWS Invoice Manager — handles invoicing for AWS Organizations payers; not a forecasting calculator for a proposed architecture's monthly list-price cost
AWS Cost Saver Report — not a documented AWS product name; no canonical AWS tool by this label estimates monthly cost of a proposed architecture
AWS Pricing Calculator — free web tool that estimates monthly cost for proposed architectures pre-deploy, using AWS public list prices for each component
questions.explanation: The AWS Pricing Calculator (calculator.aws.amazon.com) helps estimate costs upfront. Model EC2 instance types, storage, data transfer, and other services to build a cost estimate for budget approval or comparison.

nodes.title: Mixed exam topics: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Some exam objectives don't fit neatly into a single domain — they span protocols, tools, or concepts covered briefly in multiple sections. These cards treat each item as a stand-alone fact, the way an exam question presents it: one concept, one answer.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between a hub, a switch, and a router?
flashcards.back: Hub: Layer 1, repeats every frame to all ports — all devices share bandwidth, collisions guaranteed. Switch: Layer 2, forwards frames using a MAC address table to only the destination port — full duplex, no collisions, each port gets full bandwidth. Router: Layer 3, makes forwarding decisions based on IP address, connects different networks. Hub is legacy; switches dominate LAN; routers are at network edges.

flashcards.front: What is RAID 5 and how many drives can it tolerate losing?
flashcards.back: RAID 5 stripes data and parity across at least 3 drives. Any single drive failure can be recovered by reconstructing missing data from the remaining drives and parity. It cannot tolerate 2 simultaneous drive failures. Effective capacity = (N-1) × drive size. Read performance is excellent; write requires parity recalculation. RAID 6 tolerates 2 failures using double parity.

flashcards.front: What does a proxy server do, and how does a forward proxy differ from a reverse proxy?
flashcards.back: Forward proxy: sits between clients and the internet on behalf of clients — used for content filtering, caching, and anonymizing outbound requests (the server sees the proxy's IP). Reverse proxy: sits in front of servers on behalf of the server — used for load balancing, SSL termination, caching, and hiding backend topology (the client sees the proxy's IP). Both intermediate HTTP, but they protect opposite sides.

flashcards.front: What is the purpose of a DMZ in network architecture?
flashcards.back: A demilitarized zone is a network segment between the untrusted internet and the trusted internal network, typically protected by two firewalls (or two interfaces on one firewall). Public-facing services (web, email, DNS) sit in the DMZ: internet can reach them but not the internal network; if the DMZ host is compromised, the inner firewall still blocks access to the internal LAN.

questions.q: A workload runs the SAME m5.large fleet 24×7 with no changes for the next 3 years. The finance team wants the BIGGEST possible compute discount in exchange for a multi-year commitment. Which EC2 pricing model fits?
choices: On-Demand per-second pricing — pays the highest hourly rate and carries no commitment or discount in exchange for steady multi-year compute usage
Spot Instances — up to 90% off the On-Demand rate but interruptible; unsuitable for a steady multi-year workload that cannot tolerate reclaim events
Reserved Instances (or Savings Plans) with a 3-year all-upfront term — up to 72% discount in exchange for the multi-year commitment the workload already plans to make
Dedicated Hosts — physical-host isolation billing model used for licensing compliance; not the deepest-discount steady-multi-year-workload option for EC2 compute
questions.explanation: For a STEADY, multi-year workload, the deepest discount comes from 3-year all-upfront Reserved Instances (up to 72%) or Compute Savings Plans (similar). On-Demand has NO commitment and NO discount. Spot is cheaper but interruptible. PRIOR VERSION HAD WRONG CORRECT-ANSWER INDEX (marked On-Demand as the cheapest model, which is exactly backwards) — fixed 2026-05-13.

questions.q: A new AWS account holder is reading the Free Tier offer. AWS publishes three categories: ALWAYS-FREE services, 12-MONTH free usage for new accounts, and SHORT-TRIAL free for specific services. Which describes the Free Tier correctly?
choices: The Free Tier covers ALL services for the lifetime of the account, with no monthly caps or trial-period restrictions on any AWS service or region
The Free Tier mixes 12-months-free offers for new accounts, always-free monthly allowances on certain services, and short-trial offers for specific products
The Free Tier covers only EC2 t-class instances for the first 30 days and then transitions to standard On-Demand pricing across every region
The Free Tier is identical to a Reserved-Instance commitment for new accounts, locking in a 1- or 3-year discount on selected service usage
questions.explanation: AWS Free Tier includes: 12-month free (new accounts) — e.g., 750hr/month EC2 t2.micro; Always free — e.g., 1M Lambda requests/month; Trial — e.g., 2 months Amazon Redshift.

questions.q: A finance team compares EC2 cost models: (a) ~12 months of free usage on small instance types, (b) per-hour pay-as-you-go, (c) 1- or 3-year commitment with 40-72% discount, (d) interruptible spare capacity at up to 90% off. Which mapping is correct?
choices: All four EC2 cost models have the same effective hourly rate — false; Free Tier, On-Demand, Reserved, and Spot all carry different effective hourly rates and terms
Spot is dedicated long-running capacity contracted for the full life of the workload — false; Spot is interruptible spare capacity that AWS can reclaim on short notice
Reserved is more expensive than On-Demand at every comparable instance class — false; Reserved offers ~40-72% discount over On-Demand in exchange for 1- or 3-year commitment
Free Tier = 12-months free for limited usage; On-Demand = pay-as-you-go; Reserved = 1/3-yr commit with big discount; Spot = interruptible spare capacity at deep discount
questions.explanation: EC2 pricing: On-Demand (full price, flexible), RI Standard (fixed type, ~72% off, 1-3yr), RI Convertible (~66% off, can change type), Spot (bid on spare capacity, cheapest, interruptible with 2-min notice), Savings Plans (flexible commitment).

questions.q: A platform team manages 40 AWS resources across 3 environments. They want to declare the entire stack as code in JSON or YAML files, version-control it, do change-set previews before applying, and roll back on failure. Which AWS service is the native infrastructure-as-code engine?
choices: Elastic Beanstalk — managed PaaS that deploys application code from an uploaded artefact; not a general declarative IaC engine over arbitrary AWS resources
OpsWorks — managed Chef and Puppet configuration management for EC2; not a declarative IaC engine over JSON/YAML templates with change sets and drift
AWS CloudFormation — declarative JSON/YAML templates over arbitrary AWS resources, with change sets, drift detection, rollback, and stack updates
Systems Manager — fleet operations (patch, run-command, parameter store); not a declarative template-based IaC engine with change sets and drift detection
questions.explanation: AWS CloudFormation allows you to define AWS infrastructure as JSON or YAML templates and deploy it in a repeatable, automated way.

questions.q: A team needs a HIERARCHICAL key/value config + secret store for app config: dev/prod/region scoping via the path key, AT REST encryption via KMS for SecureString entries, version history per parameter, and a generous free tier. Which AWS service fits (without Secrets Manager's automatic rotation features)?
choices: AWS Secrets Manager — has rotation, but PAID per secret; the question asks for the free / config-store alternative
S3 bucket storing config files — works but no native KMS+versioning+hierarchy semantics for params
EC2 fleet manager — operational, not config storage
Systems Manager Parameter Store — hierarchical, KMS-encrypted SecureString, version history, free standard tier
questions.explanation: Parameter Store stores config data (DB strings, feature flags, AMI IDs) hierarchically (e.g., /prod/db/password). Free for standard parameters. SecureString type encrypts with KMS. Alternative to hardcoded config.

questions.q: An operations engineer wants to scale capacity based on demand for: (a) EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling Group, (b) DynamoDB read/write capacity, (c) ECS service desired-count, (d) Aurora read replicas. AWS offers a unified service that orchestrates scaling across all of these. Which?
choices: Scaling only available for EC2 — false; multiple AWS services (DynamoDB, ECS, Aurora replicas, Spot Fleet) participate in coordinated automatic scaling
AWS Compute Optimizer — recommends right-sizing of EC2 / EBS / Lambda based on usage; it does not perform automatic scale-out or scale-in actions
Elastic Load Balancing — distributes incoming requests across registered targets; it does not add or remove capacity in response to demand signals
AWS Auto Scaling — orchestrates dynamic scaling across EC2 ASG, DynamoDB, ECS, and Aurora replicas via target-tracking and step-scaling policies
questions.explanation: Auto Scaling policies: Target Tracking (e.g., CPU at 70%), Step Scaling (add 2 instances when CPU > 80%), Scheduled Scaling (predict load). Scaling out = add instances, Scaling in = remove instances.

questions.q: A team needs a managed relational database with: (a) MySQL/PostgreSQL wire-compatibility (zero application change), (b) auto-scaling storage up to 128 TB, (c) up to 15 low-latency cross-AZ read replicas, (d) standard AWS billing per second. Which managed RDS engine fits ALL four?
choices: DynamoDB — managed NoSQL key-value store; not MySQL/PostgreSQL wire-compatible and not designed for relational OLTP with classic engine compatibility
ElastiCache for Redis — in-memory key-value cache; fast but not a durable relational engine wire-compatible with MySQL or PostgreSQL clients
Amazon Aurora (MySQL- or PostgreSQL-compatible) — managed RDBMS with auto-scaling storage to 128 TB and up to 15 low-latency replicas
Amazon Redshift — petabyte-scale columnar data warehouse for analytics; not a MySQL/PostgreSQL wire-compatible transactional engine with replicas
questions.explanation: Aurora is AWS's cloud-native relational database. It auto-scales storage, replicates across 3 AZs with 6 copies, and offers serverless options. Fully managed within RDS.

questions.q: An RDS engineer compares two HA-vs-scaling options: (A) a synchronous standby in a different AZ that the engine auto-fails-over to on primary failure; (B) asynchronous COPY replicas in the same or other Region that take read traffic to scale OUT reads. Which mapping is correct?
choices: They are functionally interchangeable — false
Read Replicas are for point-in-time backup — false; automated backups are a separate feature
Multi-AZ = synchronous standby for HA failover; Read Replicas = asynchronous read-scaling replicas
Multi-AZ is for cross-Region DR — false; Multi-AZ is in-region; cross-Region is Read Replicas or Aurora Global
questions.explanation: Multi-AZ: synchronous standby in different AZ for failover HA — automatic failover ~1-2min. Read Replicas: asynchronous copies for read scaling — promotes manually for DR. Both can exist simultaneously.
